title: UN's Western Sahara mission ends after US and Russia veto each other's drafts
dek: The Security Council failed to renew MINURSO, a 35-year-old peacekeeping mission, after rival resolutions were blocked. Morocco welcomed the result; Algeria expressed 'deep regret'.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The United Nations peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara, known as MINURSO, has reached the end of its mandate after the Security Council failed to renew it, with Russia and the United States blocking each other's draft resolutions at a meeting in New York on Friday. The mandate expired on Saturday, 31 October, ending 35 years of a mission set up in 1991 to organise a referendum on the territory's future.

It is a rare outcome: UN peacekeeping mandates are usually rolled over, often with little debate, and it is unusual for a mission to lapse because the Council's permanent members cannot agree.

## What happened

According to the UN's official record of the Council's 10126th meeting, a draft tabled by the United States received 11 votes in favour, but Russia voted against it, which as a permanent member amounted to a veto. Three members abstained, among them China and Pakistan. A rival Russian draft, which would have extended the mission until 31 October 2027, won only three votes, from Russia, China and Somalia; the United States voted against it and the other 11 members abstained.

The US representative called Russia's veto "truly unfortunate", said the status quo was unacceptable and added that "any drawdown of the mission should be orderly and stable", the UN record shows. Russia's representative said the US text "could have reversed the entire resolution process" and described Moscow's own veto as "life-saving". China said a peacekeeping mandate "should not be used to exert political pressure". France warned that an abrupt closure of the mission "would be exceedingly alarming".

## How the parties reacted

Morocco, which controls most of the territory and regards it as part of its kingdom, welcomed the result. In a statement on Friday night, the Royal Office said "a 35-year chapter has now come to a close" and that the mission's presence "is expected to cease in the coming days", according to the text as published in one report. On Saturday government spokesperson Samir Belfqih told the state news agency that non-renewal was "a significant step toward closing the Sahara dispute", according to one report, and said Morocco remained committed to the ceasefire.

Algeria, which backs the Polisario Front's demand for independence, expressed "deep regret", according to a Foreign Ministry statement cited in another report. It said the US draft had been "excessively and blatantly favourable" to Morocco. No statement from the Polisario Front had been published by early Sunday, India time, and the UN Secretariat had not set out how a drawdown would be managed.

## Background

Western Sahara, a former Spanish colony on Africa's Atlantic coast, has been disputed since Spain withdrew in 1975. Morocco and the Polisario Front fought until a UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991, when MINURSO was set up to monitor the truce and prepare a referendum on self-determination. The vote never took place, as the two sides could not agree on who would be eligible.

In October 2025 the Council adopted Resolution 2797, which backed Morocco's autonomy plan as a basis for talks, a shift that Algeria and the Polisario opposed. This year's split reflects a wider breakdown between Washington and Moscow at the Council, which has also been unable to agree on Ukraine and Iran.

## Why it matters for India

India has generally said the dispute should be settled through the UN-led political process, and it was not mentioned in Friday's debate. But the episode adds to India's long-standing argument that the Security Council, dominated by five veto-holding powers, is struggling to perform even routine tasks. India is one of the largest contributors of troops to UN peacekeeping, and the lapse of a mission because of a clash between permanent members is likely to feature in its case for reform.

Morocco also matters to India economically. It is a major supplier of phosphates and phosphate fertilisers used by Indian farmers, and the two countries have expanded defence ties in recent years.

## What happens next

With no mandate in force, the mission is now expected to wind down, though the UN has not yet said how or when. The Council could still adopt a new text: any resolution would need nine votes and no veto from the five permanent members.
